topics.title: Day, month and year from the sky

learn.hook: Long before clocks and phones, people knew when to sow seeds and when to celebrate harvests just by watching the Sun, the Moon and the stars!
points: A day comes from the Earth spinning on its axis (rotation). From one sunrise to the next takes about 24 hours.
A month comes from the Moon's phases. From one new moon to the next takes about 29.5 days.
A year comes from the Earth going once around the Sun (revolution). It takes about 365¼ days, so every fourth year gets an extra day, 29 February: a leap year.
Through the year the Sun's rising point on the horizon slowly shifts north and south, and the length of shadows at noon changes. People used sticks (gnomons) and sundials to track this.

In the northern half of the Earth, the longest day comes around 21 June (summer solstice) and the shortest around 22 December (winter solstice). Around 21 March and 23 September (equinoxes), day and night are nearly equal.

example.q: Think it through: A calendar year has 365 days, but the Earth takes about 365¼ days to go around the Sun. What would happen if we never added leap days?
steps: Each year the calendar would fall about ¼ day behind the Earth's actual position.
After 4 years that adds up to about 1 day.
Over a few centuries the dates would drift by weeks, and seasons would arrive in the 'wrong' months.
example.answer: The calendar would slowly drift away from the seasons, so we add a leap day roughly every four years.

learn.reallife: The Jantar Mantar in Jaipur, built in the 1700s, has a giant sundial whose shadow tells the local time, a reminder of how India tracked time using the sky.

quiz.q: What causes day and night?
options: The Earth's rotation on its axis
The Earth's revolution around the Sun
quiz.explain: As the Earth spins, each place turns towards the Sun (day) and away from it (night).
steps: The Earth spins on its axis (rotation)
Each place turns towards the Sun (day) and then away from it (night)
Answer: The Earth's rotation on its axis
quiz.mistake: Confuses rotation with revolution

quiz.q: About how many days does the Earth take to go once around the Sun?
quiz.explain: One revolution takes about 365¼ days, which is why we have leap years.
steps: One revolution of the Earth around the Sun takes about 365¼ days
365¼ = 365.25 days, which is why we have leap years
Answer: 365.25
quiz.mistake: Mixes up the year with the month or the day

quiz.q: Which of these is a leap year?
quiz.explain: 2028 is divisible by 4 (2028 ÷ 4 = 507), so it is a leap year.
steps: A leap year is divisible by 4
2028 ÷ 4 = 507 exactly, while 2026, 2027 and 2030 are not divisible by 4
So 2028 is the leap year
Answer: 2028
quiz.mistake: Does not apply the divisible-by-4 rule

quiz.q: How many days does February have in a leap year?
quiz.explain: The extra day is added as 29 February.
steps: February normally has 28 days
In a leap year one extra day is added: 28 + 1 = 29 days
Answer: 29
quiz.mistake: Forgets which month gets the leap day

quiz.q: Around which date is the longest day of the year in India?
quiz.explain: The summer solstice in the northern half of the Earth falls around 21 June.
steps: In the northern half of the Earth the longest day is the summer solstice
It falls around 21 June
Answer: 21 June
quiz.mistake: Mixes up the summer and winter solstices

quiz.q: On an equinox, day and night are:
quiz.explain: Equinox means 'equal night'. Around 21 March and 23 September, day and night are nearly equal.
steps: Equinox means 'equal night'
Around 21 March and 23 September, day and night are nearly equal in length
Answer: Nearly equal in length
quiz.mistake: Does not know what an equinox is

quiz.q: A gnomon is a stick whose shadow helps us track time. Why does its noon shadow change length through the year?
options: The Sun's height in the noon sky changes with the seasons
Shadows change only because of clouds
quiz.explain: The Sun is higher at noon in summer and lower in winter, so noon shadows are shorter in summer and longer in winter.
steps: The Sun is higher in the noon sky in summer and lower in winter
So the gnomon's noon shadow is shorter in summer and longer in winter
Answer: The Sun's height in the noon sky changes with the seasons
quiz.mistake: Does not link shadow length with the Sun's position

quiz.q: Why do we add a leap day roughly every four years?
options: The Earth takes about 365¼ days to orbit the Sun
The Moon takes 4 years to go around the Earth
To make the year end on a Sunday
quiz.explain: Four quarter-days add up to about one whole day, which we add to keep the calendar in step with the seasons.
steps: A calendar year has 365 days but the Earth takes about 365¼ days
Four quarter-days add up to 1 day, so a leap day every four years keeps the calendar in step with the seasons
Answer: The Earth takes about 365¼ days to orbit the Sun
quiz.mistake: Does not connect the leap day with the extra ¼ day

teach.ask: Gappu asks: Who decided that a day, a month and a year are as long as they are? Did someone just guess?
teach.praise: A day is one spin of the Earth, a month is one cycle of the Moon's phases, and a year is one trip around the Sun. The sky is our clock!
teach.nudge: What does the Earth do to make a day? What does the Moon have to do with a month? And what about a year?

revise.summary: A day comes from the Earth's rotation (24 hours), a month from the Moon's phases (29.5 days) and a year from its revolution around the Sun (365¼ days), so every fourth year adds 29 February. Solstices (21 June, 22 December) give the longest and shortest days; at equinoxes day equals night.
focus: Day, month and year from rotation, Moon and revolution
Changing noon shadows and the gnomon
remember: Day ≈ 24 hours; lunar month ≈ 29.5 days; year ≈ 365¼ days
Leap year: divisible by 4, February has 29 days
Longest day ~21 June, shortest ~22 December; equinoxes ~21 March and 23 September
traps: Day and night come from rotation, not revolution
Noon shadows are shorter in summer, longer in winter
Without leap days the calendar would drift from the seasons

learn.hook: The Moon seems to grow from a thin silver smile into a full round plate and then shrink away again. But it never really changes shape!
points: The Moon has no light of its own. It shines because it reflects sunlight, and the half facing the Sun is always lit.
As the Moon goes around the Earth, we see different amounts of its lit half. These changing shapes are called phases.

Order of phases: new moon (Amavasya, Moon not visible), waxing crescent, first quarter (half moon), waxing gibbous, full moon (Purnima), waning gibbous, last quarter, waning crescent, and back to new moon.
The bright part grows (waxes) for about 15 days from new moon to full moon, called Shukla Paksha in many Indian calendars, and shrinks (wanes) for about 15 days, called Krishna Paksha.
The full cycle takes about 29.5 days. The Moon also rises about 50 minutes later each day, on average; a full moon rises around sunset.

example.q: Think it through: Tonight is full moon. About how many days until the next full moon, and what phase will you see after about a week?
steps: One complete cycle of phases takes about 29.5 days.
After full moon, the lit part starts shrinking (waning).
About a week later the Moon is half lit: the last quarter.
example.answer: About 29.5 days until the next full moon; after about a week you will see the last quarter (a half moon).

learn.reallife: Many Indian festivals are fixed by the Moon: some fall on a full-moon night and others on a new-moon night, which is why their dates change from year to year.

quiz.q: Why does the Moon shine?
quiz.explain: The Moon has no light of its own; we see sunlight bouncing off its surface.
steps: The Moon has no light of its own
We see sunlight bouncing off its surface, so it shines by reflecting sunlight
Answer: It reflects sunlight
quiz.mistake: Thinks the Moon is a light source

quiz.q: About how long is one full cycle of the Moon's phases, in days?
quiz.explain: From one new moon to the next takes about 29.5 days.
steps: From one new moon to the next
takes about 29.5 days
Answer: 29.5
quiz.mistake: Confuses the full cycle with a fortnight or a week

quiz.q: Which phase comes right after the new moon?
quiz.explain: After the new moon, a thin lit crescent appears and grows: the waxing crescent.
steps: After the new moon, a thin lit sliver appears and grows
This phase is the waxing crescent
Answer: Waxing crescent
quiz.mistake: Does not know the order of the phases

quiz.q: Why do we see phases of the Moon?
options: We see different amounts of its sunlit half as it orbits the Earth
The Earth's shadow covers part of it every night
quiz.explain: Half the Moon is always lit; the part of that lit half we can see changes as the Moon moves around the Earth.
steps: Half the Moon is always lit by the Sun
As it orbits the Earth, we see different amounts of that sunlit half
Answer: We see different amounts of its sunlit half as it orbits the Earth
quiz.mistake: Thinks phases are caused by the Earth's shadow

quiz.q: On a new-moon night (Amavasya), the Moon is:
quiz.explain: At new moon, the Moon's lit side faces away from us, so we cannot see it.
steps: At new moon, the Moon's lit side faces away from us
So on Amavasya the Moon is not visible
Answer: Not visible
quiz.mistake: Confuses new moon with full moon

quiz.q: The fortnight when the bright part of the Moon is growing is called:
quiz.explain: Shukla Paksha is the waxing (bright) fortnight; Krishna Paksha is the waning fortnight.
steps: The bright part grows (waxes) for about 15 days
This waxing fortnight is Shukla Paksha; the waning one is Krishna Paksha
Answer: Shukla Paksha
quiz.mistake: Mixes up the waxing and waning fortnights

quiz.q: On average, the Moon rises each day about:
options: 50 minutes later than the day before
quiz.explain: Because the Moon moves along its orbit, it rises about 50 minutes later each day on average.
steps: The Moon moves along its orbit each day
So on average it rises about 50 minutes later than the day before
Answer: 50 minutes later than the day before
quiz.mistake: Thinks the Moon rises at the same time every day

quiz.q: A full moon is usually seen rising:
quiz.explain: At full moon the Moon is opposite the Sun, so it rises in the east as the Sun sets in the west.
steps: At full moon the Moon is opposite the Sun
So it rises in the east as the Sun sets in the west, around sunset
Answer: Around sunset
quiz.mistake: Does not link the full moon's position with the Sun

teach.ask: Gappu hoots at the sky: Last week the Moon was a thin slice and tonight it is round! Is it growing like me?
teach.praise: The Moon reflects sunlight, and as it goes around the Earth we see more or less of its lit half. Those are phases, not growing!
teach.nudge: Where does the Moon's light come from? And what is the Moon doing that changes how much of the lit part we see?

revise.summary: The Moon shines by reflected sunlight; half of it is always lit. As it orbits the Earth we see changing amounts of the lit half: the phases, from new moon (Amavasya) to full moon (Purnima) and back. The cycle takes about 29.5 days, and the Moon rises about 50 minutes later each day.
focus: Why the Moon shines and shows phases
remember: New moon → waxing crescent → first quarter → waxing gibbous → full moon → waning gibbous → last quarter → waning crescent
Cycle ≈ 29.5 days; full moon rises around sunset
Shukla Paksha: waxing; Krishna Paksha: waning
traps: Phases are not caused by the Earth's shadow
The Moon does not change its shape or make its own light
Moonrise is about 50 minutes later each day, not at the same time

learn.hook: Why does a festival fall in October one year and November the next, while your birthday stays on the same date every year? Different calendars!
points: A solar calendar follows the Sun and the seasons. The Gregorian calendar we use for school and work is solar, with 365 days and 366 in a leap year.
A lunar calendar follows the Moon. Twelve lunar months of about 29.5 days make about 354 days, roughly 11 days shorter than a solar year.
So in a purely lunar calendar, dates slowly shift through the seasons. The Hijri calendar is an example of a lunar calendar.

A lunisolar calendar uses lunar months but adds an extra month about every two and a half to three years to keep in step with the seasons. Many traditional Indian calendars do this; the extra month is called Adhik Maas.
India's national calendar, the Saka calendar, was adopted in 1957. Its first month, Chaitra, usually begins on 22 March (21 March in a leap year).

example.q: Think it through: How many days shorter is a 12-month lunar year than a 365-day solar year? (Take a lunar month as 29.5 days.)
steps: Lunar year = 12 × 29.5 = 354 days
Difference = 365 − 354 = 11 days

learn.reallife: Wall calendars in many Indian homes show both the Gregorian date and the tithi from a traditional calendar, so families can plan both school days and festivals.

quiz.q: About how many days are there in 12 lunar months of 29.5 days each?
steps: Answer: 354
quiz.explain: Twelve lunar months add up to about 354 days.
quiz.mistake: Assumes a lunar year has the same days as a solar year

quiz.q: About how many days shorter is a 354-day lunar year than a 365-day solar year?
quiz.explain: 365 − 354 = 11 days, so lunar dates shift about 11 days earlier each solar year.
steps: Given: lunar year = 354 days, solar year = 365 days
Difference = 365 − 354
= 11 days
Answer: 11
quiz.mistake: Subtracts wrongly or guesses one month

quiz.q: Which calendar adds an extra month now and then to stay in step with the seasons?
quiz.explain: Lunisolar calendars add an extra month (Adhik Maas) about every two and a half to three years.
steps: A lunisolar calendar uses lunar months
It adds an extra month (Adhik Maas) about every two and a half to three years to stay in step with the seasons
Answer: Lunisolar calendar
quiz.mistake: Does not know how lunisolar calendars correct the drift

quiz.q: The Gregorian calendar is a:
quiz.explain: It follows the Earth's revolution around the Sun, with leap years to match about 365¼ days.
steps: The Gregorian calendar follows the Earth's revolution around the Sun
with leap years to match about 365¼ days, so it is a solar calendar
Answer: Solar calendar
quiz.mistake: Thinks our school calendar follows the Moon

quiz.q: In which year was the Saka calendar adopted as India's national calendar?
quiz.explain: India adopted the Saka calendar as its national calendar in 1957.
steps: India chose the Saka calendar as its national calendar
It was adopted in 1957
Answer: 1957
quiz.mistake: Confuses it with the year of Independence (1947) or the Republic (1950)

quiz.q: The first month of the Indian national (Saka) calendar is:
quiz.explain: Chaitra is the first month and usually begins on 22 March.
steps: The Saka calendar's first month usually begins on 22 March
That month is Chaitra
Answer: Chaitra
quiz.mistake: Does not know the national calendar's first month

quiz.q: Why do festivals fixed by a lunar or lunisolar calendar fall on different Gregorian dates each year?
options: Lunar months do not fit exactly into the solar calendar
The Sun moves faster some years
Gregorian months change length every year
quiz.explain: Lunar months (about 29.5 days) do not line up with Gregorian months, so the dates move.
steps: Lunar months are about 29.5 days long
They do not fit exactly into Gregorian months, so festival dates shift
Answer: Lunar months do not fit exactly into the solar calendar
quiz.mistake: Does not see the mismatch between lunar months and the solar year

quiz.q: The extra month in a lunisolar calendar is called:
quiz.explain: Adhik Maas means 'extra month'; it is added so festivals stay in their seasons.
steps: The extra month added to a lunisolar calendar
is called Adhik Maas, meaning 'extra month'
Answer: Adhik Maas
quiz.mistake: Confuses month names with phases of the Moon

teach.ask: Gappu scratches his head: My birthday is on the same date every year, but some festivals keep jumping around. Why?
teach.praise: My birthday follows the solar calendar, but festivals follow the Moon, and 12 lunar months are about 11 days shorter, so their dates shift. Brilliant!
teach.nudge: Which calendar follows the Sun and which follows the Moon? Are their years the same length?

revise.summary: Solar calendars like the Gregorian follow the seasons (365 or 366 days). Lunar calendars like the Hijri have 12 months of about 29.5 days, about 354 days, so dates drift about 11 days a year. Lunisolar calendars add Adhik Maas. India's Saka calendar (1957) starts with Chaitra on 22 March.
focus: Why lunar dates drift by about 11 days
remember: Lunar year = 12 × 29.5 = 354 days, about 11 days shorter than 365
Saka calendar adopted 1957; first month Chaitra, usually from 22 March
Adhik Maas added about every 2½–3 years
traps: The Gregorian calendar is solar, not lunisolar
A purely lunar calendar adds no extra month
The Saka calendar was adopted in 1957, not 1947
